name: BTree (attaswift)
baseline: A sorted Swift Array kept in order with binary-search insertion
verdict_reason: The README's own chart shows the B-tree level with a sorted Array up to tens of thousands of keys and pulling ahead only past roughly 30,000; the author says the interesting benefits start well over a hundred thousand items. The measurement is from the Swift 2-3 era, chart-only, and the library has had no commits since 2019.
tier_reason: No B-tree timings appear in text; the comparison exists only as a chart image, with no hardware, toolchain or date stated.
claimed_speedup: No B-tree numbers in text. The README says a sorted Array is about 6-7 times faster than a red-black tree up to about eighteen thousand items, that the B-tree's main benefits come at element counts well over a hundred thousand, and that cross-module generics cost a 10-200x slowdown on the Swift versions it targeted.
workload: Inserting random Int keys one at a time into a sorted Array, an Array-backed red-black tree, and an Array-backed B-tree of order 1024; 128 to 262,144 keys (chart).
one_liner: In-memory B-tree giving sorted lists, sets and maps with O(log n) insert; beats a sorted Array only at large counts.
how_it_is_fast: Each node is a small contiguous array of up to about 16 KiB of elements, so lookups binary-search cache-friendly memory and the tree stays a few levels deep. Inserting shifts elements within one node instead of the whole collection, turning the sorted Array's O(n) insertion into O(log n). Nodes are individually copy-on-write, so mutating a copy duplicates only one path.
use_it_when: Sorted collections of hundreds of thousands of elements with frequent inserts and removals
Sorted data that is copied and then mutated, where Array copies everything
Positional (rank) access into large sorted sets
skip_it_when: Fewer than tens of thousands of elements: a sorted Array was as fast or faster in the README's chart
New projects needing maintenance: no commits since 2019, written for Swift 3-4
Hot loops over simple value types, unless the code is compiled into your module or cross-module optimization specializes it
caveats: Chart-only evidence; no hardware, Swift version or date stated, and the chart predates Swift 4.2.

The '10-200x' cross-module generics penalty described in the README predates @inlinable (Swift 4.2) and cross-module optimization; the library does not use @inlinable, so modern behavior depends on compiler settings and is unmeasured.
The deeper benchmarks live in the paid Optimizing Collections book, which was not checked.
tradeoffs: More code and memory overhead than a sorted Array for small collections
Unmaintained; swift-collections' SortedSet/SortedDictionary (also B-tree based) are not yet in its stable public API

evidence.quote: Near the beginning of the curve, up to about *eighteen thousand items*, a sorted array implementation imported from an external module is very consistently about 6-7 times faster than a red-black tree
The most interesting benefits of B-trees often occur at element counts well over a hundred thousand.
Relying on `import` will incur a *10-200x slowdown* when your collection is holding these most basic value types.
